lesson.title: Prepositions as Physical Metaphors
lesson.subtitle: über↔over, unter↔under, durch↔through — and the case each one drags along

hook.title: Space Is Grammar
hook.content: The prepositions are the most physical words in German — and almost all of them are your own. über ↔ over. unter ↔ under. vor ↔ fore (before). durch ↔ through. aus ↔ out. bei ↔ by. mit ↔ mid (midwife). zu ↔ to. German describes space the way English does — it just refuses to abbreviate the case grammar: motion across a boundary drags the accusative, position drags the dative. über das Haus (over the house — flying across it) versus über dem Haus (above the house — hovering). One preposition, two cases, two physical realities.

footnotes.title: The Two-Way Prepositions
footnotes.content: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen are the Wechselpräpositionen — 'changeable prepositions'. Motion (wohin? where-to?) → accusative; location (wo? where-at?) → dative. The case answers the question you ask about the scene.

pattern.title: The Spatial Set and Its Two Cases
pattern.content:
The static set (always dative): aus (out of — Ich komme aus Berlin), bei (by/at — bei Berlin), mit (with), nach (after/to), seit (since), von (from), zu (to). The dynamic pair-set (dative location, accusative motion): in dem Haus → im Haus (in the house) vs in das Haus → ins Haus (into the house); über dem Haus (above it) vs über das Haus (over it); unter dem Tisch (under it, lying there) vs unter den Tisch (under it, going there). vor and durch complete the picture: vor dem Haus (in front of it — dative), durch den Park (through it — accusative always, motion by definition).

One Denglisch ladder, read it the German way first: Das Auto steht vor dem Haus → The car stands before to-the house → The car stands in front of the house. The middle line puts both lessons on the page: vor is before/fore, and dem is the dative 'the' the parked scene demands.
pattern.trap_note: Your mind will offer: “case is arbitrary and each preposition just takes one.” Half of them take *two*, and the case tells you whether you are sitting still (dative: in dem Haus) or moving (accusative: in das Haus). Where are you, or where are you going? The answer picks the case.
pattern.linguist_note: The contractions are the case system showing its seams: im = in + dem (dative), ins = in + das (accusative), am = an + dem, zum = zu + dem, zur = zu + der. Each contraction tells you the case before the sentence finishes.

exercises.prompt: The spatial twins — match each preposition with its English cognate:
exercises.target_answer: über, unter, durch, bei, die Ecke, die Mitte
exercises.meaning: over, under, through, by/at, the corner, the middle
exercises.explanation: The spatial prepositions are almost all twins — the V→B shift (über), the gh→ch pair (durch/through), the exact match (bei/by) — and die Ecke, die Mitte are the nouns that name the spots: an der Ecke, in der Mitte. They build time too: um Mitternacht — at midnight, the gh→ch compound on the clock.

exercises.prompt: 'Die Katze ist _____ dem Tisch.' (The cat is lying under the table — no motion):
exercises.meaning: Die Katze ist unter dem Tisch
exercises.explanation: wo? (where-at?) → dative: dem. The cat is AT REST under the table — am Strand too (the beach; strand is the shore-word English kept): location, dative. legen lays things somewhere and takes the destination: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch — lay's y→g twin, accusative on arrival.

exercises.idea: you're giving directions to a friend: you walk to the house
cues: zu + dem shrinks to zum — the contraction shows its case: Ich gehe zum Haus

vocab_hints.note: zu always takes the dative — the contraction wears it openly

exercises.explanation: The contraction is the case system showing its seams: zum = zu + dem (dative). zu never accuses — it always dates. für accuses instead: ein Buch für die Nichte — something for the niece, accusative gift.

exercises.prompt: What archaic English word (as in 'midwife') is the twin of 'mit'?
exercises.explanation: English retired 'mid' but kept it in midwife — 'with-woman'. German uses mit daily.

exercises.prompt: Which English is built the German way?
exercises.german: Das Auto steht vor dem Haus.
exercises.natural: The car stands in front of the house.
options: The car stands before to-the house.
The car stands in front of the house.
The car stands in front to-the house.
exercises.target_answer: The car stands before to-the house.
exercises.meaning: The car stands in front of the house.
exercises.explanation: Read it the German way: 'before to-the house.' vor is before/fore, and dem is the dative 'the' that a motion-less scene demands — the case is on the page, where English hides it in word order.

summary.outcome: Use the cognate prepositions and pick accusative vs dative by motion.

use_example.german: Das Auto steht vor dem Haus.
use_example.english: The car stands in front of the house.

summary.takeaway: The prepositions are your own spatial words — and the case answers the question: wohin? accusative, wo? dative.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the über, unter, durch metaphor set — spatial drills with the cognate prepositions.

twist.prompt: Same walk, but today comes first: I walk to the house becomes TODAY I walk to the house. (Something still holds position 2.)
twist.explanation: Fronting fills position 1, so gehe keeps position 2 and ich slips in behind — the verb-second law that survived thirty topics.

über.context_translation: We are speaking about / over the book.

unter.context_phrase: Die Katze ist unter dem Tisch.
unter.context_translation: The cat is under the table.
unter.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *undar — the exact twin of under; governs dative (location) and accusative (motion). [wiktionary]

vor.context_phrase: Das Auto steht vor dem Haus.
vor.context_translation: The car stands in front of the house.
vor.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *furai — the twin of English fore (before, forefather); governs dative and accusative. [wiktionary]

durch.etymology_derivation: Double shift: th → d and gh → ch.

aus.context_translation: I come from / out of Berlin.

bei.etymology_derivation: The exact twin of English by — both from Proto-Germanic *bi. Governs the dative. [wiktionary]

mit.etymology_derivation: The exact twin of archaic English mid 'with' — fossilized in midwife, 'with-woman'. Governs the dative. [wiktionary]

zu.etymology_derivation: Initial t → z [ts]. Functions as both intensifier (too) and infinitive particle (in order to).

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

tisch.context_phrase: Der Teller steht auf dem Tisch.
tisch.context_translation: The plate stands on the table.
tisch.etymology_derivation: Latin discus → Old English disc (dish/desk) → Old High German tisc (tisch, with d → t).

ecke.context_translation: I am waiting at the corner.
ecke.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *agjō — the same word as English edge. [wiktionary]

mitte.context_phrase: Ich wohne in der Mitte der Stadt.
mitte.context_translation: I live in the middle of the city.
mitte.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *midjǭ — cognate with English mid (see Mittwoch, mid-week). [wiktionary]

strand.context_translation: We are going to the beach.
strand.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *strando — the page lists English strand (shore) as the direct cognate, as in London's Strand. [wiktionary]

mitternacht.etymology_derivation: Mitter + Nacht — inherited from Proto-Germanic *midjanahts, the very same middle-night compound as English midnight. [wiktionary]

nichte.context_translation: My niece is playing in the garden.
nichte.etymology_derivation: This form replaced obsolete Niftel in the 17th century; English niece is a Latin loan of the same kinship root. [wiktionary]

legen.context_phrase: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.
legen.context_translation: I lay the book on the table.

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
